recipes.title: Saffron Lamb Tagine
recipes.description: Slow-braised lamb with saffron, preserved lemon, olives, and a mountain of warming spices. Serve over fluffy couscous.
steps: Season lamb generously with salt and ras el hanout.
Sear in a large tagine or heavy casserole until browned all over.
Add sliced onions and garlic; cook until softened.
Pour in saffron water, 300ml stock, and honey. Tuck in preserved lemon.
Cover and simmer on low for 1.5 hours until lamb falls off the bone.
Add olives for the final 15 minutes. Garnish with fresh coriander.

recipes.title: Truffle Carbonara
recipes.description: Roman classic elevated with black truffle. Silky egg and pecorino sauce, no cream ever. A lesson in restraint.
steps: Cook pasta in well-salted boiling water until al dente.
Render guanciale in a cold pan until crispy. Remove from heat.
Whisk egg yolks, whole egg, and pecorino with plenty of black pepper.
Reserve 1 cup pasta water. Drain pasta and add to pan with guanciale.
Off heat, pour egg mixture over pasta. Toss vigorously, adding pasta water to achieve silky sauce.
Finish with truffle shavings and extra pecorino.

recipes.title: Miso Black Cod
recipes.description: Nobu-inspired miso-marinated black cod. Silky, lacquered, impossibly tender. Marinate 2–3 days for best results.
steps: Whisk miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a saucepan over medium heat until sugar dissolves. Cool completely.
Pat cod dry and coat generously in marinade. Cover and refrigerate 2–3 days.
Scrape off excess marinade. Broil at high heat for 8–10 minutes until caramelised.
Serve immediately with pickled ginger and micro shiso.

recipes.title: Birria Tacos
recipes.description: Juicy braised beef birria with rich consommé for dipping. Crispy, cheesy, deeply spiced. Weekend project, weekday reward.
steps: Toast and rehydrate dried chillies. Blend with onion, garlic, chipotles, and spices into a smooth paste.
Marinate beef in the paste overnight.
Brown beef in a heavy pot. Add remaining marinade and 1L water. Simmer covered for 3 hours until shreddable.
Shred beef and strain braising liquid into a bowl (this is the consommé).
Dip tortillas in consommé, fill with beef and cheese, fold and fry in a hot skillet until crispy.
Serve with a bowl of hot consommé for dipping.

recipes.title: Butter Chicken
recipes.description: The definitive butter chicken: charred tandoori-style chicken in a velvety, mildly spiced tomato-cream sauce. Goes with everything.
steps: Marinate chicken in yoghurt and tandoori paste for at least 2 hours.
Grill or broil chicken until charred at edges. Set aside.
Fry onions in ghee until deep golden. Add garlic, ginger, and spices.
Add tomatoes; simmer 15 minutes. Blend sauce until smooth.
Return to pan, add cream and chicken. Simmer 10 minutes.
Season to taste. Finish with a knob of butter and fresh coriander.

recipes.title: Shakshuka
recipes.description: Spiced tomato sauce with perfectly set eggs, feta, and fresh herbs. Weekend breakfast turned weeknight dinner.
steps: Sauté onion and pepper until soft. Add garlic and spices; cook 1 minute.
Pour in tomatoes; simmer 10 minutes until thickened. Season well.
Create 6 wells in the sauce. Crack an egg into each.
Cover and cook on low until whites are set but yolks still runny (5–7 min).
Crumble feta over the top. Scatter fresh parsley. Serve from pan with crusty bread.

recipes.title: Pad Thai
recipes.description: Street-style pad thai: chewy rice noodles, wok-charred shrimp, tamarind sauce, crunchy peanuts. 20 minutes start to finish.
steps: Soak noodles in warm water 20 minutes until pliable. Drain.
Mix tamarind, fish sauce, and sugar into a sauce.
Heat wok until smoking. Stir-fry shrimp until pink. Push to side.
Add noodles and sauce. Toss over high heat.
Push to side, scramble eggs. Mix everything together.
Add sprouts and spring onions. Plate and top with peanuts, lime, chilli.

recipes.title: Beef Wellington
recipes.description: Gordon Ramsay would approve. Beef fillet wrapped in mushroom duxelles and golden puff pastry. The showstopper of showstoppers.
steps: Sear beef fillet all over until browned. Brush with Dijon. Chill.
Blitz mushrooms; cook in butter until all moisture evaporates. Season. Cool.
Lay prosciutto on clingfilm, spread duxelles, roll beef tightly. Refrigerate 30 min.
Wrap in puff pastry, seal edges, brush with egg wash. Score top decoratively.
Bake at 220°C for 25–28 minutes until pastry is deep golden.
Rest 10 minutes before slicing to serve.

recipes.title: Kenyan Beef Stew
recipes.description: Kenyan Beef Stew is the ultimate comfort dish — tender beef slow-simmered in a rich tomato gravy with onions, garlic, ginger, and warm spices. Found on nearly every Kenyan family table, it is the perfect companion to ugali, chapati, or rice.
recipes.longDescription: Every Kenyan home has its version of beef stew, and every version tells a story. The secret is patience — browning the beef first for deep caramelised flavour, then simmering low and slow until the meat practically falls apart in the gravy. Prepared for Sunday lunches, celebrations, and ordinary weekday dinners alike, this is the dish that makes a house smell like home.
ingredients: 1 kg stewing beef — cut into 3–4 cm cubes
2 tbsp tomato paste — optional but recommended
2 tbsp fresh coriander — chopped, for garnish
steps: Wash the beef, pat it completely dry with a cloth, and season lightly with salt and black pepper.
Heat the oil in a heavy sufuria over medium-high heat until shimmering.
Brown the beef in batches — do not crowd the pot. Sear each batch until deeply caramelised on all sides, then remove and set aside. This step builds the entire foundation of flavour.
In the same pot, add the onions and cook over medium heat until deeply golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger, stirring for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the chopped tomatoes and tomato paste. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the tomatoes completely break down into a thick, dark sauce — about 10 minutes.
Return the browned beef to the pot, stirring to coat every piece in the tomato base.
Pour in the beef stock and bring to a gentle boil.
Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 60–75 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is nearly tender.
Add the carrots and bell pepper during the last 20 minutes of cooking.
Continue simmering uncovered for the final 10 minutes to thicken the gravy to your liking.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Garnish generously with fresh coriander and serve hot.
chefTips: Use beef with some marbling — chuck or shin cuts give the richest, most tender result.
Never skip the browning step — it adds a depth of flavour you simply cannot get any other way.
Simmer gently, never boil rapidly — a rolling boil will toughen the beef.
Make it the day before — beef stew always tastes even better the next day as the flavours deepen overnight.
commonMistakes: Cooking on high heat throughout — makes the beef tough and dry.
Skipping the browning step — results in a flat, grey stew without depth.
Adding all vegetables at the start — carrots and peppers will turn to mush.
Too little liquid — causes the bottom to scorch before the beef is tender.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently on the stovetop over low heat, adding a splash of water or stock if the sauce has thickened. Alternatively microwave in short intervals, stirring between each.

recipes.title: Kenyan Layered Chapati
recipes.description: Kenyan Chapati is a soft, flaky, pan-cooked flatbread beloved across the country. Its signature delicate layers come from a simple technique of rolling, oiling, folding, and coiling the dough before cooking. Served at breakfast, celebrations, and everyday meals, chapati is one of Kenya's most treasured breads.
recipes.longDescription: Few things in a Kenyan kitchen bring as much satisfaction as a perfectly layered chapati — golden on the outside, soft and flaky within. The technique of coiling the dough before re-rolling is the heart of it, trapping thin layers of oil between sheets of dough that separate beautifully during cooking. Chapati carries the gentle influence of South Asian cuisine woven into Kenyan food culture over generations, and today it appears on tables from the coast to the highlands, at weddings, Christmas, Eid, and quiet Sunday mornings alike.
ingredients: 1 tbsp sugar — optional, for light golden browning
6 tbsp vegetable oil — for the dough
5 tbsp vegetable oil — for layering and frying
steps: Combine the flour, salt, and optional sugar in a large bowl. Add the 6 tbsp of oil and mix until it is evenly distributed and the flour feels slightly crumbly.
Gradually pour in the warm water while mixing, bringing the dough together until it is soft, smooth, and not sticky. Add water slowly — you may not need all of it.
Knead the dough firmly for 10–12 minutes until it becomes smooth, elastic, and springs back when poked.
Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 30 minutes. This step is essential — do not skip it.
Divide the rested dough into 10 equal balls.
Roll one ball into a thin circle about 25 cm wide using a lightly oiled surface.
Lightly brush the surface of the circle with oil.
Fold or roll into a long strip, then coil it tightly into a spiral like a snail shell. Pinch the end underneath to seal.
Let the coiled dough rest for 5–10 minutes, then gently roll it back into a round chapati — the layers will stay intact inside.
Heat a dry frying pan (tawa) over medium heat until hot.
Place the chapati on the dry pan and cook for about 1 minute until bubbles start to form.
Flip and brush the cooked side lightly with oil. Flip again, oil the second side, and continue turning until both sides are evenly golden with visible flaky spots — about 3–4 minutes total.
Remove from the pan while hot and gently clap between your hands or squeeze with a clean towel to separate the beautiful flaky layers.
Repeat with remaining dough, keeping finished chapatis covered to stay warm and soft.
chefTips: Resting the dough is non-negotiable — it relaxes the gluten and makes rolling much easier.
Use warm water, not cold — it produces a more elastic, pliable dough.
Go easy on flour when rolling — too much dries out the chapati. Use a lightly oiled surface instead.
Cook over medium heat always — high heat burns the outside before the inside cooks through.
Clapping the chapati while still hot separates the layers dramatically. Do not skip this step.
commonMistakes: Skipping the resting period — the dough will resist rolling and tear.
Using cold water — produces a stiff, less pliable dough.
Rolling the dough too thick — results in dense, doughy chapatis.
Cooking on high heat — the outside burns while the inside stays raw.
Over-oiling — makes the chapatis greasy and heavy.
recipes.storage: Room temperature in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Refrigerate for up to 5 days. Freeze for up to 2 months — separate each chapati with parchment paper.
recipes.reheating: Warm on a dry frying pan for 1–2 minutes per side, or microwave briefly under a damp paper towel to restore softness.

Offers moderate protein (6g per chapati) from wheat flour.
Can be made with whole-wheat flour to significantly increase fibre content.
Pairs beautifully with vegetables and protein-rich stews for a complete, balanced meal.

recipes.title: Traditional Kenyan Githeri
recipes.community: Originally associated with the Kikuyu, Embu, and Meru communities; now enjoyed nationwide
recipes.description: Githeri is one of Kenya's most iconic traditional dishes — maize and beans slow-cooked until tender, then sautéed with onions, tomatoes, and simple seasonings into a deeply nourishing, affordable, and satisfying meal enjoyed across the entire country.
recipes.longDescription: Githeri has deep roots in central Kenya, where maize and beans have long been staple crops. Traditionally cooked in large batches over wood fires for farming communities and family gatherings, it remains today a symbol of nourishment, simplicity, and resilience. From school canteens to home kitchens to roadside stalls, githeri feeds Kenya. Add a ripe avocado on the side and it becomes something quietly extraordinary.
ingredients: 2 cups (350g) dried red beans — rosecoco or kidney beans

substitutions.alternative: Black beans, pinto beans, or cowpeas

equipment: Large cooking pot or pressure cooker
steps: Wash the maize and beans thoroughly under cold running water.
Soak them separately overnight (8–12 hours) to reduce cooking time and improve digestibility. Drain and rinse well.
Combine the soaked maize and beans in a large pot and cover generously with fresh water.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer until both are completely tender — about 90 minutes. Add water as needed to keep them submerged. (Pressure cooker: 35 minutes.)
Drain any excess water and set aside.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat.
Add the onions and cook, stirring, until soft and lightly golden — about 6–8 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in the tomatoes and cook until they break down into a thick sauce — about 6 minutes.
Add the cooked maize and beans to the pan. Season with salt, black pepper, and curry powder if using.
Mix thoroughly and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, allowing all the flavours to come together beautifully.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Scatter with chopped fresh coriander and serve hot.
chefTips: Soaking overnight is the single most important step — it dramatically cuts cooking time and makes the beans easier to digest.
Cook until the beans are just tender with a slight bite — not mushy. Texture is everything in githeri.
Add diced carrots or bell peppers when sautéing for extra colour, nutrition, and sweetness.
A ripe avocado served alongside is one of the great simple pleasures in Kenyan food.
commonMistakes: Skipping the overnight soak — dramatically increases cooking time and affects texture.
Overcooking the maize and beans until they become mushy.
Under-seasoning — githeri needs generous salt to bring out its earthy depth.
Adding tomatoes before the onions have softened — results in a raw, harsh flavour.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently on the stovetop with a splash of water, or microwave until piping hot, stirring halfway through.
healthBenefits: High in plant-based protein — 15g per serving from the maize and bean combination.
Excellent source of dietary fibre (12g per serving) — supports digestive health.
Rich in iron and folate — essential for healthy blood and energy.
Provides slow-release complex carbohydrates for lasting energy throughout the day.
Naturally cholesterol-free and low in saturated fat.

recipes.title: Kenyan Nyama Choma
recipes.community: National — especially associated with the Maasai, Kalenjin, Kikuyu, and Kamba communities
recipes.description: Nyama Choma — Swahili for 'roasted meat' — is Kenya's national barbecue tradition. Goat meat seasoned simply to honour its natural flavour, then grilled slowly over glowing charcoal until tender, juicy, and kissed with smoke. The centrepiece of every Kenyan celebration.
recipes.longDescription: Nyama Choma is more than a meal — it is a social tradition. Friends, families, and colleagues gather at nyama choma joints and home gardens every weekend, sharing freshly grilled meat eaten by hand, accompanied by kachumbari and cold drinks. The act of eating together symbolises hospitality, celebration, and community in a way that few dishes in the world can match. Goat is the traditional and most beloved choice, though beef, lamb, and chicken all have their place on the grill.
ingredients: 2 kg bone-in goat meat — cut into large pieces
2 tbsp vegetable oil — optional, for moisture

substitutions.alternative: Beef ribs, lamb chops, or chicken pieces

steps: Trim excess fat from the meat, leaving some for flavour and moisture during grilling.
Pat the meat completely dry with a cloth or paper towels.
Rub the meat all over with salt, black pepper, crushed garlic, grated ginger, and lemon juice.
Cover and marinate in the refrigerator for at least 2 hours — overnight gives deeper, more complex flavour.
Light the charcoal and allow it to burn until fully covered with a light layer of white ash. This is when it is ready — you want glowing coals, not open flames.
Arrange the coals for medium, even heat. Lightly oil the grill grate to prevent sticking.
Place the meat on the grill, leaving space between each piece for even heat circulation.
Cook slowly over medium charcoal heat, turning every 10–15 minutes. Patience is the entire secret to great nyama choma.
Baste lightly with oil if the meat begins to dry out on the surface.
Continue grilling for 50–60 minutes depending on the size of the cuts, until the meat is deeply coloured, tender, and cooked through.
Remove from the grill and rest for 5–10 minutes before serving. This is non-negotiable — resting keeps the juices inside.
Serve immediately with kachumbari, ugali, and your choice of accompaniments.
chefTips: Charcoal grilling is not optional for authentic nyama choma — it is the source of that irreplaceable smoky depth.
Never rush the fire. Cook over glowing white-ash coals, never open flames, which char the outside while leaving the inside raw.
Rest the meat before serving — cutting too early loses all the precious juices you worked 60 minutes to develop.
Keep seasoning simple — nyama choma is about the quality of the meat and the smoke, not a complex marinade.
commonMistakes: Cooking over open flames instead of glowing charcoal — burns the outside, leaves inside raw.
Turning the meat too often — disrupts crust formation and extends cooking time.
Cutting into the meat immediately after grilling — all the juices run out.
Over-seasoning — heavy marinades mask the natural flavour of the meat.
Using very lean meat — some fat is essential for flavour and to prevent drying out.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Freeze for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently on a grill, in an oven at 180°C, or in a covered pan over low heat until warmed through. Avoid microwave if possible — it toughens the meat.
healthBenefits: Rich in high-quality complete protein — 39g per serving.
Excellent source of iron, zinc, and vitamin B12 — essential for energy and immunity.
Naturally low in carbohydrates — 2g per serving.
When served with sukuma wiki and ugali, forms a complete and balanced meal.

The tradition of eating together by hand, tearing the meat apart at the table, is a powerful expression of Kenyan hospitality and community that no formal dining setting can replicate.

recipes.title: Kenyan Kachumbari
recipes.description: Kachumbari is Kenya's most vibrant and refreshing side dish — ripe tomatoes, thinly sliced red onions, fresh coriander, chilli, and a bright squeeze of lemon juice, tossed together into a salad that cuts through rich grilled meat like sunshine through clouds.
recipes.longDescription: You will find kachumbari on virtually every table where nyama choma is being served. It provides the perfect counterpoint — cool, crisp, and acidic against the smoky, charred richness of the meat. Every household and restaurant has its own version, but the heart of it never changes: ripe tomatoes, sharp onion, coriander, and citrus. Simple food that asks only for good ingredients and a little patience.
ingredients: 3 tbsp freshly squeezed lemon or lime juice

substitutions.alternative: Bird's eye chilli, or omit for a milder salad

steps: Wash all vegetables thoroughly under cold running water.
Dice the tomatoes into neat, bite-sized pieces. Use a sharp knife to keep them clean-edged rather than crushed.
Thinly slice the red onions. If you prefer a milder flavour, soak the sliced onions in cold water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat dry.
Finely chop the coriander and chilli.
Place the tomatoes, onions, coriander, and chilli in a large mixing bowl.
Add the lemon juice, olive oil if using, salt, and black pepper.
Toss gently until everything is evenly combined — do not overmix or the tomatoes will break apart.
Let the salad rest for 10 minutes before serving to allow the flavours to meld beautifully.
Serve chilled or at room temperature alongside nyama choma, ugali, or any grilled dish.
chefTips: Use ripe but firm tomatoes — overripe tomatoes release too much liquid and make the salad watery.
Soaking sliced onions in cold water for 10 minutes removes sharpness while keeping the crunch.
Add diced avocado just before serving for a richer, creamier version.
Prepare shortly before serving — kachumbari is best when the vegetables are still crisp and fresh.
commonMistakes: Using overripe tomatoes — they release too much water and the salad becomes soggy.
Chopping vegetables unevenly — uniform cuts make the salad look and eat better.
Overmixing — causes the tomatoes to break down and lose their texture.
Adding salt too far in advance — draws moisture out of the tomatoes and dilutes the dressing.
recipes.storage: Best enjoyed fresh. Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 24 hours.
recipes.reheating: Not applicable — serve chilled or at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants from fresh tomatoes and citrus.
Very low in calories — just 55 kcal per serving.
Good source of dietary fibre supporting healthy digestion.

It is a dish that requires no cooking, no special equipment, and almost no time — yet it elevates every plate it touches.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Beef Pilau
recipes.community: National — particularly popular along the Kenyan Coast
recipes.description: Kenyan Beef Pilau is a fragrant, deeply spiced one-pot rice dish that stands as one of the country's most celebrated recipes. Tender beef, deeply caramelised onions, basmati rice, and a hand-ground blend of cumin, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, and pepper all come together into something that smells like a celebration.
recipes.longDescription: Pilau has a long and storied history on the Kenyan coast, shaped by centuries of Indian Ocean trade that brought Persian, Indian, and Arab culinary traditions to East Africa. Over generations it became embraced across the entire country and is now the centrepiece of weddings, Eid, Christmas, birthdays, and family gatherings from Mombasa to Nairobi. The defining element is patience — deeply browned onions, toasted whole spices ground fresh, and rice that is never stirred while it cooks.
ingredients: 4 cups (800g) basmati rice — washed and soaked 20 minutes

substitutions.alternative: High-quality pre-made pilau spice blend (2 tbsp)

equipment: Spice grinder or mortar and pestle
steps: Toast the cumin seeds, peppercorns, cardamom pods, cloves, and cinnamon stick in a dry pan over low heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring constantly, until deeply fragrant. Do not let them burn.
Remove from heat and allow to cool completely. Grind to a fine powder using a spice grinder or mortar and pestle. Mix in the ground coriander and set aside.
Heat the oil or ghee in a large heavy sufuria over medium heat. Add the sliced onions.
Cook the onions slowly, stirring frequently, until they are deep, rich golden brown — about 20–25 minutes. This is the most important step for pilau colour and flavour.
Add the garlic and ginger, stirring for 1–2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the beef and brown on all sides over medium-high heat.
Sprinkle in the pilau spice mix and stir for 2 minutes, coating every piece of beef in the aromatic blend.
Add the tomatoes if using and cook until they soften and break down — about 5 minutes.
Pour in the hot beef stock and bring to a gentle boil. Cover and simmer for 40–50 minutes until the beef is completely tender.
Taste the broth and adjust salt. Add the soaked, drained basmati rice and stir gently once to distribute evenly.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to the lowest possible setting. Cover tightly with a lid (place a sheet of foil under the lid for a tighter seal if needed).
Cook undisturbed for 20–25 minutes. Do not lift the lid or stir during this time.
Remove from heat and allow the pilau to rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
Uncover, fluff gently with a fork, garnish generously with fresh coriander, and serve immediately.
chefTips: The onions are everything — take the full 20–25 minutes to caramelise them to deep golden brown. This gives pilau its signature colour and sweetness.
Toast your own whole spices and grind them fresh. The difference in aroma versus pre-ground spice blends is extraordinary.
Never stir the rice while it cooks — this breaks the grains and makes the pilau starchy and clumped.
Rest the pilau for 10 minutes after cooking before fluffing. Steam continues cooking the rice gently to perfection.
commonMistakes: Not browning the onions deeply enough — results in pale, flat-tasting pilau.
Using too much water — makes the rice mushy and ruins the texture.
Burning the spices by toasting on high heat — creates bitterness.
Stirring the rice too often during cooking — breaks grains and makes the pilau starchy.
Rushing the beef — undercooked beef ruins the entire dish.

recipes.title: Kenyan Chicken Pilau
recipes.community: National — especially popular along the Coast and in urban households
recipes.yieldDesc: Approximately 2 kg of cooked chicken pilau
recipes.description: Kenyan Chicken Pilau is a lighter, faster cousin of the celebrated beef pilau — fragrant basmati rice cooked with tender chicken, deeply caramelised onions, and the same warming blend of cumin, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, and pepper that makes Kenyan pilau unmistakable.
recipes.longDescription: Where beef pilau demands hours of slow braising, chicken pilau is the weeknight celebration — still deeply aromatic, still built on those beautifully browned onions and freshly toasted spices, but ready in under 90 minutes. Bone-in chicken pieces give the broth a richness that elevates every grain of rice. Along the Kenyan coast, this dish carries centuries of Swahili culinary tradition in every spoonful.
ingredients: 1.2 kg bone-in chicken pieces — preferred for a richer broth
4 cups (800g) basmati rice — washed and soaked 20 minutes

substitutions.alternative: Turkey or firm tofu with vegetable stock for a vegetarian version

equipment: Spice grinder or mortar and pestle
steps: Toast the cumin seeds, cardamom pods, cloves, peppercorns, and cinnamon stick in a dry pan over low heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring continuously, until deeply fragrant.
Allow to cool completely, then grind to a fine powder. Mix in the ground coriander and set aside.
Heat the oil or ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the sliced onions.
Cook the onions slowly, stirring often, until they are deep golden brown — about 20–25 minutes. This is the heart of great pilau.
Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the pilau spice blend and cook for 1 minute, letting the spices bloom in the oil.
Add the chicken pieces and brown lightly on all sides — about 5 minutes.
Add the tomatoes if using and cook until softened — about 5 minutes.
Pour in the hot chicken stock. Cover and simmer for 25–30 minutes until the chicken is nearly cooked through.
Add the soaked, drained basmati rice. Stir gently once to distribute evenly. Taste the broth and adjust the salt.
Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat to the lowest setting. Cover tightly and cook undisturbed for 20–25 minutes.
Remove from heat. Rest covered for 10 minutes, then fluff gently with a fork, garnish with fresh coriander, and serve.
chefTips: Bone-in chicken pieces give the broth far more flavour than boneless — use them whenever possible.
Brown the onions deeply to a rich golden — this colour and sweetness is the defining character of authentic pilau.
Use aged basmati rice if you can find it — the grains stay longer and fluffier.
Never stir the rice after adding it. Never lift the lid during cooking. Trust the steam.
commonMistakes: Overcooking the chicken before adding rice — it will become dry by the time the rice is done.
Too much liquid — causes soggy, clumped rice.
High heat after adding rice — burns the bottom while the top stays raw.
Skipping the spice toasting — raw whole spices have a flat, harsh flavour.

recipes.title: Traditional Kenyan Mukimo
recipes.description: Mukimo is a traditional Kenyan mashed dish that brings potatoes, maize, peas, and leafy greens together into something deeply comforting. Smooth yet textured, earthy yet light — it is the taste of Central Kenya at its most generous.
recipes.longDescription: Mukimo has been a cornerstone of Kikuyu cuisine for generations, born from the fertile highlands of Central Kenya where potatoes, maize, and leafy greens grow abundantly. Traditionally prepared after harvests using whatever was freshest from the farm, it represents the spirit of using what the land gives you and making it beautiful. Today it travels far beyond its origins, served across Kenya as a beloved companion to beef stew, nyama choma, and fried fish.
ingredients: 2 cups (300g) fresh maize kernels — or frozen sweet corn
1 cup (150g) green peas — fresh or frozen
250g pumpkin leaves or spinach — washed and chopped
½ cup (120ml) milk — optional, for creaminess

substitutions.alternative: Plant-based milk or reserved cooking water
Broad beans or shelled pigeon peas

steps: Peel, wash, and quarter the potatoes.
Place the potatoes, maize kernels, and peas into a large pot. Cover with cold water and add 1 tsp of salt.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and cook for 25–30 minutes until the potatoes are completely soft when pierced with a knife.
In the last 5–7 minutes of cooking, add the chopped pumpkin leaves or spinach. Stir them in and let them wilt and cook through — do not overcook or they will lose their vibrant green colour.
Drain most of the cooking water, reserving a cupful in case you need it for mashing.
Add the butter and milk if using.
Mash everything together using a potato masher or wooden mwiko. The goal is a smooth but textured mixture — small pieces of maize and flecks of green should remain visible. Do not over-mash.
Taste and season with the remaining salt and black pepper.
Mix well to ensure the greens and maize are evenly distributed throughout.
Serve hot alongside beef stew, nyama choma, or any rich accompaniment.
chefTips: Use floury potatoes (not waxy) for a fluffy, light mash rather than a gluey one.
Add the greens in the last 5 minutes only — overcooking turns them khaki and destroys their nutrients.
Leave visible pieces of maize and flecks of green — this is the traditional texture. Over-mashing loses what makes mukimo distinctive.
For a richer version, replace the milk with a splash of fresh cream.
commonMistakes: Using waxy potatoes — they produce a dense, gluey mash instead of a light, fluffy one.
Adding too much liquid — makes the mukimo runny and hard to serve.
Over-mashing until completely smooth — removes the characteristic texture of traditional mukimo.
Forgetting to season after mashing — the mixture needs final salt adjustment.
Overcooking the greens — they turn dull and lose their colour and nutrients.

heritage.origin: Central Kenya — Kikuyu community
heritage.history: Mukimo has its roots in the agricultural traditions of the Kikuyu people of Central Kenya. Historically prepared after harvests using freshly picked maize, potatoes, and greens from family farms, it was a dish of abundance and community. Traditionally cooked in a large clay pot over an open fire and mashed with a wooden mwiko, mukimo was shared at harvest celebrations, family gatherings, and communal feasts.
heritage.modernEvolution: While the traditional method used pumpkin leaves and fresh-harvested maize, modern versions across Kenya often use spinach or sukuma wiki, frozen peas and corn, and add butter or cream for a richer texture. Mukimo is now found in restaurants and catered events throughout the country.

recipes.title: Traditional Kenyan Irio
recipes.description: Irio is a traditional Kikuyu dish of coarsely mashed potatoes, sweet maize, green peas, and leafy greens — rustic by design, with each ingredient still visible in the finished dish. Hearty, nourishing, and deeply rooted in the highlands of Central Kenya.
recipes.longDescription: Where Mukimo aims for a smoother, more unified mash, Irio celebrates texture — each green pea, each sweet kernel of maize, each fleck of spinach should be visible in the final dish. This is the rustic, honest food of the central highlands, born from harvest abundance and prepared with a light hand. Coarsely mashed and simply seasoned, Irio has fed Kikuyu families for generations and continues to comfort and nourish across all of Kenya today.
ingredients: 2 cups (300g) fresh maize kernels — fresh or frozen
1½ cups (225g) green peas — fresh or frozen

substitutions.alternative: Reserved cooking water or plant-based milk

steps: Peel and wash the potatoes, cutting them into even quarters so they cook at the same rate.
Place the potatoes, maize kernels, and peas into a large pot. Cover with cold water, add 1 tsp of salt, and bring to a boil.
Cook for 25–30 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender when pierced with a knife.
Add the chopped spinach or pumpkin leaves in the final 5 minutes of cooking. Stir through and allow to wilt — do not overcook.
Drain most of the cooking water, reserving a cupful in case it is needed for mashing.
Add the butter and milk if using.
Mash gently with a potato masher — the goal is a coarse, rustic texture. Some whole peas, visible maize kernels, and green flecks should remain. This is what makes irio distinct from a smooth mash.
Taste and season with the remaining salt and black pepper.
Mix gently until evenly combined. Serve hot.
chefTips: Use starchy potatoes — they give a lighter, fluffier result than waxy varieties.
The coarse texture is intentional and traditional — do not over-mash. Visible peas and corn are correct.
Freshly harvested maize gives the best natural sweetness. If using frozen, thaw and drain well first.
Add chopped spring onions after mashing for an extra layer of fresh flavour.
commonMistakes: Mashing until completely smooth — this makes it Mukimo, not Irio. The rustic texture is the point.
Overcooking the greens — they turn dull and lose their nutrients and colour.
Adding too much liquid — makes the irio runny and impossible to serve neatly.
Forgetting to taste and adjust seasoning after mashing — the mixture needs a final salt check.

heritage.origin: Central Kenya — Kikuyu community, Kenya's central highlands
heritage.history: Irio has nourished Kikuyu families for generations, rooted in the agricultural rhythms of the central highlands where potatoes, maize, peas, and leafy greens grow side by side. Traditionally prepared during harvest seasons using freshly picked ingredients, it was a dish that celebrated the land's abundance. Cooked in clay pots over wood fires and mashed with a wooden mwiko, irio was central to communal meals, family gatherings, and celebrations tied to the harvest calendar.
heritage.modernEvolution: Modern irio frequently uses spinach in place of pumpkin leaves, frozen peas and corn for convenience, and may include butter or cream for richness. It has spread far beyond the Kikuyu heartland and is now served in restaurants across Kenya, often listed alongside Mukimo as a traditional side dish.

Both celebrate the same highland ingredients; the difference is in texture and regional emphasis.

recipes.title: Samaki wa Kupaka
recipes.description: Samaki wa Kupaka is the jewel of Kenya's Swahili coast — a whole fish scored, marinated in garlic, ginger, and lemon, grilled over charcoal until smoky and tender, then coated in a rich, golden coconut milk sauce fragrant with turmeric, coriander, and chilli. A dish that tastes of the Indian Ocean.
recipes.longDescription: From Mombasa to Lamu, Samaki wa Kupaka tells the story of the Swahili coast in a single dish — centuries of Arab, Persian, and Indian Ocean trade woven into every spoonful of coconut sauce. The technique of grilling the fish first over charcoal before bathing it in coconut milk is the defining move: the smoke of the grill and the richness of the coconut create a flavour combination that is entirely, unmistakably coastal Kenyan.
ingredients: 1 whole tilapia, snapper, or kingfish (1–1.2 kg) — cleaned and scored on both sides

substitutions.alternative: Freshly grated coconut blended with warm water

steps: Score the fish on both sides with 3–4 deep diagonal cuts to allow the marinade to penetrate.
Rub the fish all over — inside the cavity and into the cuts — with the crushed garlic, grated ginger, lemon juice, salt, and black pepper.
Cover and refrigerate for 30 minutes to marinate.
Heat your charcoal grill to medium heat. Grill the fish for 8–10 minutes per side until just cooked through with a light char on the skin.
While the fish grills, heat the oil in a saucepan over medium heat.
Add the onion and cook until soft and translucent — about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and tomato, cooking until the tomato breaks down completely into a soft sauce.
Stir in the turmeric, paprika, and chilli. Cook for 1 minute to bloom the spices.
Pour in the coconut milk. Reduce heat and simmer gently for 5 minutes, stirring. Do not boil vigorously or the coconut milk will separate.
Stir in the chopped fresh coriander. Taste and adjust salt.
Remove the fish from the grill. Brush the coconut sauce generously over both sides.
Return the fish to the grill for a final 3–5 minutes, allowing the coconut sauce to caramelise lightly into the skin.
Serve immediately with extra coconut sauce on the side.
chefTips: Fresh fish is everything — the best Samaki wa Kupaka starts with the freshest fish you can find.
Simmer the coconut milk gently, never boil it hard — high heat causes it to split and lose its creamy richness.
Charcoal grilling gives the authentic smoky depth. A gas grill works but lacks that coastal character.
Brush the coconut sauce on in the final minutes only — too early and it burns before the fish is ready.
commonMistakes: Overcooking the fish until it becomes dry and falls apart.
Boiling the coconut sauce on high heat — it separates and becomes oily.
Skipping the marinade — the fish needs at least 30 minutes to absorb the flavour.
Using thin, watery coconut milk — thick coconut milk is essential for a rich sauce.

heritage.origin: Kenyan Swahili Coast — Mombasa, Lamu, and the Indian Ocean coastline
heritage.history: Samaki wa Kupaka is one of the great dishes of Swahili coastal cuisine, born from centuries of Indian Ocean trade that brought Arab, Persian, and Indian culinary traditions to East Africa. The marriage of grilled fish with coconut milk sauce — enriched with turmeric, coriander, and chilli — reflects the layered cultural history of Kenya's coast, where spice routes shaped not just commerce but daily life and the food people cook. In coastal homes from Mombasa to Lamu, this dish is prepared for family meals, seaside gatherings, and celebrations.
heritage.modernEvolution: While traditionally prepared over a charcoal jiko with freshly grated coconut, modern versions use canned coconut milk and gas or oven grills without losing the essence of the dish. Kingfish and snapper remain popular coastal choices, though tilapia is widely used inland.

It is commonly prepared for family meals, seaside gatherings, and festive occasions from Mombasa to Lamu.

recipes.title: Traditional Kenyan Omena Stew
recipes.description: Omena is one of Western Kenya's most iconic traditional foods — small silver fish from Lake Victoria, sun-dried, then lightly fried and simmered in a rich tomato and onion sauce. Deeply flavourful, packed with protein and calcium, and served with ugali in virtually every Luo household.
recipes.longDescription: Omena carries the smell and soul of Lake Victoria in every bite. These tiny dried fish — barely a few centimetres long, eaten bones and all — are one of Kenya's great nutritional treasures. Frying them first in hot oil tames the strong aroma before they are simmered into a thick, fragrant tomato sauce. For millions of Kenyan families, a pot of omena with ugali is not just a meal — it is home.
ingredients: ½ tsp salt — use sparingly, dried omena can already be salty
steps: Sort through the dried omena carefully, removing any debris or damaged fish.
Rinse quickly under cold water and drain well. Do not soak or overwash.
Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat.
Add the omena and fry for 3–5 minutes, stirring gently, until lightly crisp and aromatic. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, add the onions and cook until soft and lightly golden — about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in the diced tomatoes and tomato paste. Cook for 6–8 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a thick sauce.
Return the fried omena to the pan. Stir gently to combine.
Add a small splash of water if the sauce looks too thick. Simmer gently for 8–10 minutes.
Taste carefully before adding any salt — dried omena is often already salty.
Stir in the fresh coriander, adjust seasoning, and serve hot.
chefTips: Do not soak the omena or overwash it — a quick rinse is enough.
Frying the omena before stewing is not optional — it transforms the aroma and texture.
Taste before adding salt — dried omena is already salty and easy to over-season.
A squeeze of fresh lemon just before serving adds brightness beautifully.
commonMistakes: Overwashing the omena — removes the distinctive flavour.
Adding too much salt — dried fish is already naturally salty.
High heat after adding tomatoes — burns the sauce before it develops.
Overcooking — the omena becomes too dry and loses its pleasant texture.

heritage.history: Omena — the silver cyprinid fish harvested from Lake Victoria — has sustained the Luo fishing communities of Western Kenya for generations. Traditionally sun-dried along the lakeshore to preserve the catch through the seasons, omena became a reliable, affordable source of protein and calcium for families across the region.
heritage.modernEvolution: Once considered a regional staple, omena has spread to every corner of Kenya through migration and urbanisation. It is now sold in markets and supermarkets across the country and has earned recognition for its exceptional nutritional value.

recipes.title: Kenyan Maharagwe ya Nazi
recipes.description: Maharagwe ya Nazi is one of Kenya's most comforting vegetarian dishes — red kidney beans slowly simmered in thick, creamy coconut milk with onions, tomatoes, garlic, ginger, and warm spices. A Swahili coastal classic that turns simple ingredients into something truly special.
recipes.longDescription: Along Kenya's Indian Ocean coast, coconut milk is not a luxury — it is a daily ingredient, and maharagwe ya nazi is one of the most beloved ways to use it. The beans absorb the sweetness and richness of coconut milk as they simmer, creating a stew that is deeply satisfying without a single piece of meat. It is the kind of food that smells like the coast — warm, fragrant, and welcoming.
ingredients: 500g dried red kidney beans — soaked overnight and cooked until tender
400ml thick coconut milk — fresh or canned

substitutions.alternative: Black beans, cannellini beans, or pigeon peas
Fresh coconut cream diluted with water

equipment: Large cooking pot or pressure cooker
steps: Wash the dried kidney beans and soak overnight in plenty of cold water.

Drain, rinse, and place in a large pot. Cover with fresh water and cook until completely tender — about 60–75 minutes, or 30–35 minutes in a pressure cooker. Drain, reserving 1 cup of the cooking liquid.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the onions and cook, stirring, until soft and lightly golden — about 6–8 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the diced tomatoes and tomato paste. Cook for 6–8 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a thick, rich sauce.
Add the curry powder and turmeric. Stir for 1 minute to bloom the spices in the oil.
Add the cooked beans and reserved cooking liquid. Stir gently to coat the beans in the sauce.
Pour in the coconut milk and mix gently. Do not stir vigorously.
Reduce heat to low and simmer for 10–15 minutes, stirring occasionally. Do not boil hard — this causes the coconut milk to split.
For a thicker stew, use the back of a spoon to lightly mash a small portion of the beans against the side of the pan.
Season with salt and black pepper. Allow to rest for 10 minutes off the heat.
Finish with fresh chopped coriander and serve hot.
chefTips: Use freshly extracted coconut milk if you can — the flavour difference over canned is remarkable.
Simmer gently after adding the coconut milk — high heat causes it to separate and become oily.
Mashing a small portion of the beans naturally thickens the stew without any added starch.
Let the stew rest for 10 minutes before serving — the flavours deepen noticeably.
commonMistakes: Not soaking the dried beans overnight — results in uneven cooking and tougher skins.
Boiling the coconut milk vigorously — it splits and the stew becomes oily rather than creamy.
Overseasoning before the stew has reduced — always taste at the end.
Using undercooked beans — they must be completely tender before adding to the sauce.

regionalMap.alsoCommonIn: Nationwide — widely enjoyed in homes across all Kenyan regions

heritage.history: Maharagwe ya Nazi is a cornerstone of Swahili coastal cuisine, born from centuries of Indian Ocean trade that brought spices, coconuts, and culinary traditions from Arabia, India, and Persia to East Africa. Along Kenya's coast, where coconut palms line the shoreline and coconut cream is a daily cooking staple, this creamy bean stew has nourished families for generations. It is affordable, deeply nutritious, and beloved for the way coconut milk transforms humble beans into something extraordinary.
heritage.modernEvolution: While traditionally made with freshly extracted coconut milk from grated coconuts, modern versions use canned coconut milk without losing the essence of the dish. Maharagwe ya Nazi has spread far beyond the coast and is now prepared in homes and restaurants across all of Kenya.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Mandazi
recipes.description: Mandazi is one of Kenya's most beloved fried breads — lightly sweet, fluffy, and fragrant with coconut milk and cardamom. Enjoyed for breakfast, tea time, and celebrations across the country, it is the Swahili Coast's most delicious gift to the rest of Kenya.
recipes.longDescription: Every Kenyan who has grown up around tea time knows the smell of mandazi frying — that warm, cardamom-spiced, lightly coconutty aroma that means something good is about to happen. Unlike Western doughnuts, mandazi is not excessively sweet. It has a mildly sweet, tender interior and a slightly crisp golden shell, and it is perfect with a hot cup of chai. From Mombasa to Nairobi to Kisumu, mandazi is everywhere.
ingredients: 1 tsp ground cardamom — freshly ground preferred

substitutions.alternative: ¼ cup plain yogurt for a softer texture

steps: In a large bowl, combine the sifted flour, sugar, baking powder, ground cardamom, and salt. Whisk together well.
In a separate bowl, mix together the coconut milk, warm milk, beaten egg, melted butter, and vanilla extract.
Gradually pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients, mixing as you go. Bring together into a soft dough.
Knead the dough on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes until smooth, soft, and elastic. The dough should not stick to your hands.
Place the dough in a clean bowl, cover with a damp cloth, and rest at room temperature for 1 hour. This is essential for a light, fluffy result.
After resting, lightly flour your work surface. Divide the dough into portions and roll to approximately 1 cm thick — not thinner.
Cut into triangles, diamonds, or squares using a knife or pastry cutter.
Heat the cooking oil in a deep pan to approximately 170–175°C. To test: drop a small piece of dough in — it should rise to the surface and turn golden within 30 seconds.
Fry a few pieces at a time, without overcrowding the pan. Cook for 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden brown.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.
Serve warm with chai, coffee, or alongside maharagwe ya nazi.
chefTips: Resting the dough for a full hour is non-negotiable — it develops gluten and creates the characteristic fluffy interior.
Oil temperature is everything — too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks; too cool and they absorb excess oil. 170–175°C is the sweet spot.
Never overcrowd the pan — it drops the oil temperature and results in greasy, uneven mandazi.
Freshly ground cardamom from whole pods has a dramatically better aroma than pre-ground. Worth the extra step.
commonMistakes: Oil too hot — outside browns before the inside cooks through.
Over-kneading the dough — develops too much gluten and makes mandazi tough.
Rolling the dough too thin — results in flat, crispy rather than fluffy mandazi.
Adding too much flour during kneading — makes the dough stiff and the mandazi dense.
Skipping the resting period — the dough needs time to relax for a light result.

regionalMap.alsoCommonIn: Every corner of Kenya — sold at roadside kiosks, markets, schools, and homes nationwide

heritage.origin: Kenyan Swahili Coast — with roots in Arab and Indian Ocean trade
heritage.history: Mandazi originated along the Kenyan coast as part of the rich Swahili food culture shaped by centuries of Indian Ocean trade. The use of coconut milk and cardamom reflects the spice trade routes that connected East Africa with Arabia, Persia, and the Indian subcontinent. From coastal homes to inland towns, mandazi spread across Kenya through migration, trade, and cultural exchange until it became one of the most recognisable everyday foods in the country.
heritage.modernEvolution: While the traditional version uses freshly extracted coconut milk and is fried over a charcoal jiko, modern mandazi is made across Kenya with canned coconut milk and gas stoves. Bakeries, kiosks, and cafes sell mandazi alongside chai throughout the day.

relatedDish.note: Mandazi and Mahamri are often confused but are distinct recipes. Mandazi uses baking powder and has a denser, firmer crumb, while Mahamri uses yeast giving it a lighter, airier texture and a richer coconut flavour. Mahamri puffs more dramatically during frying and is the more traditional coastal celebration bread. Mandazi is the quicker, everyday nationwide favourite.

recipes.title: Authentic Swahili Mahamri
recipes.description: Mahamri is the Swahili coast's most celebrated fried bread — lighter than mandazi, richer with coconut milk, and fragrant with cardamom. Made with yeast so it puffs dramatically during frying, it is the centrepiece of coastal breakfasts, Ramadan mornings, and Eid celebrations.
recipes.longDescription: The key difference between mahamri and mandazi is the yeast — and that difference is everything. Where mandazi is quick and everyday, mahamri requires patience: the dough needs time to rise, to develop flavour, to become something that puffs beautifully in hot oil into a light, pillowy, coconut-scented bread. Along the Kenyan coast, the smell of mahamri frying before the morning prayer during Ramadan is one of the most evocative aromas in Swahili food culture.
ingredients: 2¼ tsp (7g) instant dry yeast — 1 standard packet
250ml (1 cup) thick coconut milk — lukewarm, not hot
1 large egg — optional but traditional in many households
1½ tsp ground cardamom — freshly ground preferred
2 tbsp vegetable oil — for the dough

substitutions.alternative: Whole milk (less traditional but works well)
Omit entirely for a vegan version
Brown sugar for a richer flavour

steps: In a large bowl, combine the sifted flour, sugar, instant yeast, ground cardamom, and salt. Mix well.
Add the lukewarm coconut milk, egg (if using), and vegetable oil. Mix together.
Gradually add the warm water, a little at a time, until a soft, slightly sticky dough comes together. You may not need all the water.
Knead the dough on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes until smooth, elastic, and springy when poked.
Place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a clean damp cloth, and leave in a warm place to rise for 1½ hours until doubled in size.
Punch down the risen dough gently to release the air.
Divide into two portions. Roll each to approximately 1 cm thick on a lightly floured surface.
Cut into triangles or diamonds using a knife or pastry cutter.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 170°C. Test with a small piece of dough — it should float and turn golden within about 30 seconds.
Fry a few pieces at a time, without crowding, for 2–3 minutes per side until puffed, golden, and cooked through.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels. Serve warm.
chefTips: The proofing time is not optional — yeast needs the full 1½ hours to create the light, airy texture that makes mahamri special.
Coconut milk must be lukewarm, not hot — hot liquid kills the yeast and the dough will not rise.
Freshly ground cardamom from whole pods is dramatically more fragrant than pre-ground — worth crushing in a mortar.
Fry over steady medium heat. If the oil is too hot the outside burns before the inside cooks; too low and they become greasy.
commonMistakes: Adding coconut milk that is too hot — kills the yeast and the dough won't rise.
Not proofing long enough — results in dense, flat mahamri instead of light and puffy.
Frying at too high a temperature — burns the outside before the inside cooks through.
Rolling the dough too thin — produces flat, crispy pieces rather than fluffy mahamri.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Viazi Karai
recipes.description: Viazi Karai is Mombasa's most beloved street food — boiled potatoes coated in a lightly spiced gram flour batter, deep-fried until crisp and golden, then served with a tangy, fragrant tamarind coconut chutney. A snack that tastes like the Indian Ocean coast itself.
recipes.longDescription: Stand on any busy street in Mombasa's Old Town in the late afternoon and the smell of viazi karai frying will find you before you find the stall. The crispy golden batter, fragrant with turmeric and cumin, gives way to a soft, tender potato inside. The real star, though, is the chutney — tamarind, fresh coconut, garlic, and coriander blended into something tangy, sweet, and deeply addictive. This is the flavour of the Kenyan coast at its most joyful.
ingredients: 6 medium potatoes (about 1 kg) — peeled and halved or cut into thick wedges
½ tsp turmeric — optional, for colour

substitutions.alternative: Fresh lemon juice with a little brown sugar

steps: Peel the potatoes and cut into halves or thick wedges — uniform size ensures even cooking.
Boil in salted water (with turmeric if using) for 12–15 minutes until just tender when pierced with a knife. They should hold their shape — do not overboil.
Drain thoroughly and allow to cool completely before battering. Warm potatoes will make the batter slide off.
Make the batter: whisk together the gram flour, rice flour, baking powder, turmeric, cumin, paprika, and salt.
Gradually add the water while whisking until a smooth, thick batter forms. It should coat the back of a spoon and cling to the potatoes. Stir in the chopped coriander.
Make the chutney: blend the tamarind paste, grated coconut, brown sugar, garlic, coriander, and a splash of water until smooth. Adjust consistency and seasoning to taste.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 175°C. Test by dropping a small amount of batter — it should sizzle immediately and rise to the surface.
Dip each potato piece into the batter, coating it evenly. Let excess drip off.
Carefully lower into the hot oil. Fry in small batches — 4–6 pieces at a time — for 3–4 minutes until deep golden brown and crisp.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.
Serve immediately with the tamarind coconut chutney on the side.
chefTips: Cool the potatoes completely before battering — warm potatoes release steam which prevents the batter from adhering properly.
The batter must be thick enough to coat and cling — if it runs off easily, whisk in a little more gram flour.
Fry in small batches to maintain oil temperature. Overcrowding cools the oil and produces greasy, soggy batter.
Fresh coconut makes the best chutney by far. If using desiccated coconut, soak in warm water for 10 minutes first.
commonMistakes: Overboiling the potatoes until they fall apart — they must hold their shape in the hot oil.
Batter too thin — slides off the potato instead of creating a crisp coating.
Oil temperature too low — the batter absorbs oil and becomes greasy instead of crisp.
Skipping the chutney — it is not optional. Viazi karai without tamarind chutney is incomplete.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Bhajia
recipes.community: Popular nationwide — with strong Indian-Kenyan influence
recipes.description: Bhajia is one of Kenya's most beloved snacks — wafer-thin potato slices coated in a spiced gram flour batter fragrant with turmeric, cumin, garlic, and fresh coriander, then fried until irresistibly crispy and golden. Found on every street corner from Mombasa to Nairobi.
recipes.longDescription: The difference between good bhajia and great bhajia comes down to two things: the slice and the batter. The potatoes must be thin enough to cook through in the time it takes the batter to turn golden — a mandoline or very sharp knife is your best friend. The batter must be thick enough to cling but thin enough to become crackling crispy in the oil. Get both right and you will understand why Kenyans queue for bhajia every day.
ingredients: 4 large potatoes (about 800g) — peeled and very thinly sliced (2–3 mm)
2 cups (240g) gram flour (besan / chickpea flour) — sifted
¼ cup (30g) rice flour — for extra crispiness
¼ cup fresh coriander — finely chopped
About 1½ cups (360ml) water — to make the batter

substitutions.alternative: Omit entirely for a mild version

steps: Peel and wash the potatoes. Slice very thinly — about 2–3 mm. A mandoline slicer gives the most consistent results.
Pat the potato slices thoroughly dry with paper towels. Moisture is the enemy of crispy bhajia.
Make the batter: combine the gram flour, rice flour, turmeric, ground cumin, ground coriander, paprika, baking powder, and salt in a bowl. Mix well.
Add the minced garlic, grated ginger, chopped fresh coriander, and green chilli if using.
Gradually whisk in the water until a smooth, medium-thick batter forms. It should coat a spoon and cling to the potato slices without being so thick it clumps. Let the batter rest for 5 minutes.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 175°C. Test by dropping in a small amount of batter — it should sizzle immediately, turn golden in about 30–40 seconds.
Working in batches, dip each potato slice into the batter, shake off the excess, and lower carefully into the hot oil.
Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning once halfway, until deep golden brown and crisp all over.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack or paper towels. A wire rack keeps the base crispy better than paper towels alone.
Serve immediately while hot with tamarind chutney, pili pili sauce, or fresh lemon wedges.
chefTips: The thinner the slice, the crispier the bhajia — aim for 2–3mm. Thick slices produce a soft, starchy centre.
Rice flour is the secret weapon for crispiness — do not skip it.
Always fry in small batches. Crowding the pan drops the oil temperature and produces greasy, soggy bhajia.
Rest the batter for 5 minutes after mixing — it allows the gram flour to hydrate fully and the batter to thicken slightly.
commonMistakes: Slicing potatoes too thick — they don't cook through before the batter browns.
Batter too runny — slides off the potato and doesn't create a crispy shell.
Overcrowding the fryer — lowers oil temperature and produces oily results.
Not drying the potato slices — moisture prevents the batter from adhering properly.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Mishkaki
recipes.description: Mishkaki are Kenya's most beloved grilled beef skewers — tender cubes of beef marinated in garlic, ginger, lemon, paprika, cumin, and coriander, then charcoal-grilled until smoky, juicy, and irresistible. Found at roadside grills from Nairobi to Mombasa every evening.
recipes.longDescription: Every Kenyan town has its mishkaki grill — that corner where the charcoal smoke drifts into the street and the smell of marinated meat draws you in before you even see the stall. Mishkaki is simpler than nyama choma but no less satisfying: smaller cubes of beef, a more complex marinade, a quicker cook. It is the street food that feeds Nairobi's evening commuters, the snack at every outdoor gathering, the skewer you eat standing up with kachumbari and chapati.
ingredients: 1 kg beef sirloin or rump — cut into 2–3 cm cubes
12–15 wooden or metal skewers — soak wooden ones for 30 minutes before use

substitutions.alternative: Goat, lamb, or boneless chicken thighs
Smoked paprika for a deeper flavour

steps: In a large bowl, combine the oil, lemon juice, minced garlic, grated ginger, paprika, cumin, coriander, black pepper, salt, cayenne (if using), and fresh coriander. Mix well.
Add the beef cubes and turn to coat every piece thoroughly in the marinade.
Cover tightly and refrigerate for at least 2 hours — overnight gives the deepest, most complex flavour.
Soak wooden skewers in cold water for 30 minutes to prevent burning. Metal skewers need no preparation.
Thread the marinated beef evenly onto the skewers, leaving small gaps between the pieces so heat can circulate and the meat cooks evenly rather than steaming.
Preheat the charcoal grill to medium-high heat. The coals should be glowing with a light layer of white ash — not open flames.
Grill the skewers for 10–15 minutes total, turning every 3–4 minutes, until evenly browned on all sides with light charring at the edges.
For medium doneness, the internal temperature should reach 63°C. Cook to 70°C for well done.
Remove from the grill and rest for 5 minutes before serving — this keeps the juices inside the meat.
Serve with kachumbari, chapati, pili pili sauce, and fresh lemon wedges.
chefTips: Overnight marinating is not required but makes a dramatic difference — the spices penetrate the meat far more deeply.
Charcoal is not negotiable for authentic mishkaki — the smokiness is part of the flavour profile that gas cannot replicate.
Do not overcrowd the skewers — leave small gaps so the meat grills rather than steams.
If using remaining marinade for basting, boil it for 2 minutes first to ensure food safety before brushing it over cooked meat.
commonMistakes: Using very lean beef with no marbling — dries out quickly on the grill.
Skipping the marinating time — the spices need time to penetrate.
Cooking over open flames instead of glowing coals — burns the outside while the inside stays raw.
Turning too often — prevents a proper crust from forming on each side.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Masala Chai
recipes.description: Chai ya Maziwa — Kenyan Masala Chai — is the most universally loved drink in the country. Black tea, whole milk, fresh ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves simmered together into something rich, creamy, warming, and completely irresistible. Every Kenyan home has its own version.
recipes.longDescription: Kenya is one of the world's great tea-producing nations — the highlands of Kericho and Nandi grow black tea of extraordinary quality, exported across the globe. But the best cup of Kenyan tea is not found in an export container — it is found in a enamel mug at a roadside kiosk at 7am, fragrant with ginger and cardamom, sweet, milky, and steaming. Chai is not just a drink in Kenya. It is hospitality. It is how you greet a guest, end a hard day, and begin every morning.
ingredients: 500ml whole milk — full-fat preferred for richness
2 tbsp Kenyan black tea leaves — Kenyan tea gives the best colour and flavour
2-inch piece fresh ginger — peeled and crushed

substitutions.alternative: Low-fat milk or oat milk for a lighter version

steps: Pour the water into a medium saucepan and bring to a gentle boil over medium heat.
Add the crushed ginger, cardamom pods, cinnamon stick, whole cloves, and black peppercorns if using.
Reduce heat and simmer for 5 minutes to fully infuse the spices into the water. The water should turn a light golden colour.
Add the black tea leaves. Simmer for 2–3 minutes. Do not overboil the tea or it will become bitter.
Pour in the whole milk and stir well to combine.
Add the sugar and stir until dissolved.
Bring the chai almost to a boil, then reduce heat immediately. Simmer gently for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. Watch carefully — milk can boil over quickly.
Taste and adjust the sweetness.
Strain through a fine tea strainer into cups or a teapot.
Serve hot, ideally with mandazi, mahamri, or chapati.
chefTips: Kenyan black tea is the gold standard for this recipe — it gives a richer colour and more robust flavour than most commercial tea bags.
Simmer, never boil hard — vigorous boiling makes the tea bitter and can cause the milk to scorch on the bottom of the pan.
Crush the whole spices rather than grind them — this releases aroma without making the chai too strongly spiced.
Every Kenyan family has its own chai ratio. Start with this recipe and adjust ginger, spice, and sweetness to make it your own.
commonMistakes: Overbrewing the tea leaves — produces bitter, astringent chai.
Too many spices — overpowers the tea rather than complementing it.
Letting the milk boil over — watch the pot during the final simmer.
Forgetting to strain — loose tea leaves and whole spices must be removed before serving.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Coconut Rice
recipes.description: Wali wa Nazi is the Swahili coast's most fragrant side dish — basmati rice cooked entirely in creamy coconut milk until each grain is infused with a subtly sweet, rich coconut flavour. The perfect companion to grilled fish, coconut curries, and bean stews.
recipes.longDescription: There is nothing complicated about Wali wa Nazi — its genius is in its simplicity. Replace the water with coconut milk, and plain rice transforms into something fragrant, creamy, and completely distinctive. Along Kenya's Indian Ocean coast, this rice has been cooked for generations as the natural companion to seafood and spiced stews. Once you have eaten Samaki wa Kupaka alongside a bowl of this coconut rice, plain rice feels like a compromise.
ingredients: 2 cups (400g) long-grain basmati rice — rinsed until water runs clear
400ml thick coconut milk — fresh or canned
1 tbsp coconut oil or butter — optional

substitutions.alternative: Jasmine rice or long-grain white rice
Freshly extracted coconut milk for the most authentic flavour
Omit or use a pinch of ground cardamom
A small bay leaf for a different aroma

steps: Rinse the rice several times under cold running water until the water runs completely clear. This removes excess starch and ensures fluffy, separate grains.
Drain the rice thoroughly.
In a medium saucepan, combine the coconut milk, water, salt, cardamom pods, and cinnamon stick if using.
Bring the mixture to a gentle boil over medium heat, stirring once to combine.
Add the rinsed, drained rice. Stir once gently.
Reduce the heat to the lowest setting. Cover the saucepan tightly with a lid.
Cook undisturbed for 18–20 minutes until all the liquid has been absorbed. Do not lift the lid or stir.
Remove from heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. This allows the steam to finish cooking the rice gently and evenly.
Remove the cardamom and cinnamon. Fluff gently with a fork and serve.
chefTips: Rinse the rice thoroughly — removing surface starch is the single most important step for fluffy, separate grains.
Never stir the rice after adding it to the liquid — stirring releases starch and creates a sticky, clumped result.
Fresh coconut milk gives an incomparably richer flavour than canned. If you can find fresh coconuts, it is worth the effort.
The 10-minute rest after cooking is not optional — it allows the steam to redistribute evenly through the rice.
commonMistakes: Too much liquid — makes the rice mushy and waterlogged rather than fluffy.
Lifting the lid during cooking — releases steam and disrupts the cooking process.
Cooking on high heat after adding rice — burns the bottom before the top is cooked.
Skipping the resting period — the rice won't fully finish cooking and will be unevenly done.

heritage.origin: Kenyan Swahili Coast — born from Indian Ocean trade that brought coconuts and rice culture together
heritage.history: Wali wa Nazi is one of the most ancient dishes in Swahili coastal cuisine — the meeting point of two ingredients that the Indian Ocean trade routes made abundant on the East African coast: rice from Asia and coconuts that grow everywhere along the shoreline. For centuries, coastal families have cooked their rice in coconut milk as a matter of course, the result being a dish that is simple yet deeply fragrant and satisfying. It remains the essential side dish for seafood, curries, and bean stews throughout the Kenyan coast.
heritage.modernEvolution: While traditionally made with freshly extracted coconut milk using a hand-cranked grater, modern Wali wa Nazi uses canned coconut milk without losing its essential character. It is now served in restaurants and homes throughout Kenya, wherever Swahili cuisine is cooked.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Sprinkle with a little water and reheat gently in a microwave or on the stovetop over low heat, stirring once halfway through.
healthBenefits: Provides complex carbohydrates from rice for sustained energy.
Coconut milk contributes healthy medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs).
Naturally dairy-free and gluten-free.
A satisfying, nutrient-dense accompaniment to protein-rich seafood and bean dishes.
recipes.culturalNote: Wali wa Nazi is a cornerstone of Swahili cuisine along Kenya's Indian Ocean coast. With coconuts growing abundantly in coastal regions, the ingredient became central to local cooking through centuries of Indian Ocean trade. Today it is served at weddings, Eid celebrations, family feasts, and everyday coastal meals — almost always alongside seafood or coconut-based curries. It is the rice that makes the meal coastal.

Coconut rice with cardamom — the most aromatic version.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Kuku wa Nazi
recipes.description: Kuku wa Nazi is the jewel of Swahili coastal cooking — chicken slowly simmered in creamy coconut milk with onions, tomatoes, garlic, ginger, and warm spices until the sauce is rich, golden, and deeply fragrant. Always served with Wali wa Nazi. Always celebrated.
recipes.longDescription: There is a reason Kuku wa Nazi is prepared for every important occasion along the Kenyan coast — weddings, Eid, family homecomings. The combination of chicken simmering in coconut milk with turmeric, coriander, and garlic creates something that is simultaneously comforting and festive. The sauce turns a deep gold, thick and fragrant, clinging to every piece of chicken. Set it next to a bowl of Wali wa Nazi and you have one of the great meal combinations in all of Kenyan cuisine.
ingredients: 1.5 kg chicken — cut into serving pieces, bone-in preferred
500ml thick coconut milk — fresh or canned
¼ cup fresh coriander — chopped, for garnish

substitutions.alternative: Chicken thighs or drumsticks for a quicker cook
Freshly extracted coconut milk for the most authentic flavour

equipment: Large cooking pot or Dutch oven
steps: Wash and pat the chicken pieces completely dry. Season lightly with salt and black pepper.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken pieces for 5–7 minutes, turning, until lightly golden on all sides. This step builds deep flavour. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add the onions and cook over medium heat, stirring, until soft and lightly golden — about 6–8 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the diced tomatoes and tomato paste. Cook for 6–8 minutes until the tomatoes completely break down into a thick sauce.
Add the curry powder, turmeric, ground coriander, cumin, and paprika. Stir for 1 minute to bloom the spices in the sauce.
Return the browned chicken pieces to the pot. Stir to coat every piece in the spiced tomato base.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir gently to combine.
Bring to a gentle simmer. Reduce heat to low, cover, and cook for 35–40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is completely tender and cooked through.
Do not boil vigorously — this causes the coconut milk to separate.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and pepper.
Remove from heat and allow to rest for 10 minutes. Scatter with fresh coriander and serve with Wali wa Nazi.
chefTips: Bone-in chicken develops a far richer, deeper flavour in the sauce than boneless cuts — always worth it.
Brown the chicken properly before simmering — this golden crust adds flavour that infuses the entire curry.
Simmer gently, never boil — vigorous boiling causes the coconut milk to split into an oily, grainy sauce.
Rest the curry for 10 minutes before serving — the flavours deepen noticeably in this time.
commonMistakes: Boiling the coconut milk vigorously — it separates and the sauce becomes oily rather than creamy.
Skipping the browning step — the chicken and sauce lack depth of flavour.
Adding the spices too late — they need time to bloom and cook into the sauce.
Overcooking the chicken until it falls apart — it should be tender but still hold its shape.

heritage.origin: Kenyan Swahili Coast — shaped by centuries of African, Arab, Persian, and Indian culinary exchange
heritage.history: Kuku wa Nazi is one of the defining dishes of the Kenyan coast, born from the same centuries of Indian Ocean trade that shaped all of Swahili cuisine. In homes from Mombasa to Lamu, this dish has been prepared for weddings, Eid celebrations, and family gatherings for generations, always served alongside Wali wa Nazi.
heritage.modernEvolution: While traditionally cooked in clay pots over charcoal with freshly extracted coconut milk, modern Kuku wa Nazi uses canned coconut milk and gas stoves without losing its essential character. It is now widely served in coastal restaurants and Swahili homes across Kenya.

When served with Wali wa Nazi and kachumbari, forms a complete, balanced meal.

Lamu-style — heavier on cloves and cardamom for a more aromatic curry.

recipes.title: Authentic Kenyan Muthokoi
recipes.community: Ameru, Embu, and Kikuyu — also enjoyed in neighbouring communities
recipes.description: Muthokoi is one of Kenya's oldest and most nourishing traditional dishes — dehulled maize slowly cooked with beans until tender, then finished with a simple sauté of onions, tomatoes, garlic, and fresh coriander. Simple, deeply satisfying, and rooted in generations of highland farming tradition.
recipes.longDescription: Before there were supermarkets and packaged foods, there was Muthokoi — the result of families gathering together to pound dried maize, removing the outer husks by hand, then cooking the soft inner kernels with beans into a dish that could sustain a family through long working days. The dehulled maize has a uniquely satisfying texture, tender yet slightly chewy, that plain maize cannot replicate. It is the kind of food that feels like heritage — honest, nourishing, and deeply connected to the land.
ingredients: 2 cups (400g) dehulled maize (muthokoi) — cleaned and rinsed
1 cup (200g) dried beans — red kidney or rosecoco beans

substitutions.alternative: Red kidney beans, pinto beans, or cowpeas

steps: Wash the dehulled maize thoroughly and soak the dried beans overnight (8–12 hours). Drain and rinse both.

Place the dehulled maize in a large pot. Cover generously with water (about 6 cups) and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer for 1½ hours, adding more water as needed, until the maize kernels are tender but still hold their shape.
Meanwhile, in a separate pot, cook the soaked beans in fresh water for 60–90 minutes until completely tender. Drain and set aside.
Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook until translucent — about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds.
Stir in the diced tomatoes. Cook for 6–8 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a thick sauce.
Add the cumin, black pepper, and salt. Stir for 1 minute.
Add the cooked maize and beans to the pan. Stir gently to coat everything in the tomato sauce.
Simmer together for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, allowing the flavours to meld.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot.
chefTips: Cook the maize until tender but not mushy — it should have a pleasant chewiness.
A pressure cooker dramatically reduces cooking time — maize in 25 minutes, beans in 20.
Add fresh coriander only at the very end to preserve its bright flavour and colour.
A splash of vegetable or beef stock instead of plain water adds depth without overwhelming the traditional taste.
commonMistakes: Skipping the overnight bean soak — dramatically increases cooking time and affects texture.
Overcooking until the beans completely fall apart — they should be tender but intact.
Not seasoning adequately — maize and beans both need generous salt.
Letting the pot dry out during the long maize simmer — keep adding water.
